name: What AI Is, in Plain Terms
title: What AI Is, in Plain Terms
answer: Artificial intelligence is software that learns patterns from large amounts of data and uses them to make a guess. Schools meet two kinds, predictive AI that estimates what is likely and generative AI that produces new content. The key limit is that generative tools are built to sound right, not to know whether what they produce is true.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: This idea explains AI in plain terms so school staff and families can tell apart tools that estimate from tools that create. Predictive AI looks at data and produces a number, a list, or a flag, such as which students may miss too many days, which bus routes can be combined, or how many lunches the cafeteria will serve on Friday. Schools have used these tools for years, often without calling them AI. Generative AI produces new content, including a paragraph, a lesson plan, a translated letter, a picture, or a spoken reply. Tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude belong here, and they work by predicting which words usually come next rather than looking up an answer.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the first practical step is to sort each tool into predictive or generative. Predictive tools support estimates and lists, so they might be used for attendance patterns, bus route planning, or cafeteria counts. Generative tools support content creation, so they might be used to draft a paragraph, a lesson plan, a translated letter, a picture, or a spoken reply. The text does not give grade bands, so this distinction applies across the school rather than to one age group. Staff can ask what the tool outputs, a number, list, or flag for predictive AI, or new content for generative AI, and then treat the result accordingly.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no study, figure, or evidence label for this idea. It presents a plain explanation of how AI works rather than reporting research findings. This idea therefore rests on practice and explanation rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets a clear limit: a generative AI tool does not look up answers the way a librarian would, and it does not know whether what it wrote is true. It is built to sound right, and most of the time sounding right and being right line up. Sometimes they do not, and the tool gives no warning when they split. That means a person must decide whether to trust or act on the output, especially when it is used for a letter, a lesson plan, or any statement of fact. Predictive AI also only estimates what is likely, so its numbers, lists, and flags are not final judgments.
